Tempting, because the spokesperson is brushing off critics. But the argument never mentions the pharmacists' interests or motives. It doesn't attack them at all; it just points to someone else's approval.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The pharmacists only object because the protocol creates more work for them, so their concerns don't count.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The objection is specifically about withdrawal. Other side effects aren't part of the dispute.
The spokesperson doesn't say 'there's no proof of withdrawal, so there's none.' The reason given is the board's approval, a positive (if bad) piece of evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No study has shown this taper causes withdrawal, so it doesn't.

choices.note: Backwards. That's closer to the pharmacists' worry. The spokesperson isn't assuming fast means unsafe; if anything, the opposite.

questions.stimulus: Lena Corvo has anchored the evening news on Channel 6 for fifteen years, and in surveys the city's viewers consistently name her the most trustworthy broadcaster in the city. Corvo recently said on the air that the city's proposed transit tax would drive many small businesses out of the downtown area. So the transit tax would drive many small businesses out of the downtown area.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Dr. Pell is the most experienced cardiologist at Linden Hospital, and she has concluded that Mr. Haas's irregular heartbeat requires surgery. So Mr. Haas's irregular heartbeat requires surgery.
Most residents of Garvin believe that the town's old mill is unsafe to enter. So the old mill is probably unsafe to enter, and the town should close it.
Gerta Haan is the region's most respected wine critic, and she has called the Ostler vineyard's newest red undrinkable. So the Ostler vineyard will not sell much of its newest red.
The novelist Hugo Rane has written many bestselling mysteries, but his grasp of economics is weak. So the claims in his recent essay on trade policy must be false.

Critics consistently call Tomas Brede's violin performances flawless, and audiences admire his candor in interviews. Brede has said that the bridge being built over the Arlen River is unsafe. So the bridge is unsafe.
questions.explanation: The stimulus accepts a claim about economics because the person making it is trusted and skilled in an unrelated field, broadcasting. E does the same: a violinist's acclaim and candor are taken to settle a question of engineering. C is the most tempting trap, but Haan is judging wine, which is her field; that argument's problem is the jump from her opinion to sales, a different flaw.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The transit tax would drive many small businesses out of downtown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corvo, a long-serving and highly trusted news anchor, said so.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Person is trusted/accomplished in field F; person asserts a claim about unrelated field G; so the claim is true.

breakdown.analysis: Being a trusted anchor makes Corvo good at reading the news, not at predicting what a tax does to small businesses. Her trustworthiness means she probably isn't lying, but she can sincerely be wrong outside her area. The match needs three pieces: 1. an authority whose credentials are in one field; 2. a claim in a different field; 3. a conclusion that flatly accepts the claim.

choices.note: A cardiologist judging a heart problem is speaking inside her field. That's a reasonable appeal to authority, not the flaw in the stimulus.
This is an appeal to popularity (what most residents believe), not to one person's misplaced expertise. It also adds a recommendation the stimulus doesn't have.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most people think garlic cures colds, so it does.

choices.note: Tempting: a respected expert, a strong opinion, a confident conclusion. But Haan is a wine critic judging wine, which is her field. The flaw here is jumping from 'a critic hates it' to 'it won't sell.' That's a different gap.
This attacks the novelist's competence to reject his claims, concluding they're false. The stimulus goes the other way: it uses irrelevant credentials to accept a claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: That senator failed algebra, so her budget figures must be wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. A violinist's acclaim and candor (like Corvo's trustworthiness) are used to accept a claim about bridge engineering, a field where he has no shown expertise. Same structure, same flaw.

questions.stimulus: Greenhouse manager: Our Cassel orchids have begun to wilt. Dr. Mira Tesh, who has spent thirty years studying Cassel orchids in the cloud forests where they grow wild, says that when a Cassel orchid wilts, the cause is almost always too much water. Since no one knows Cassel orchids better than Dr. Tesh, our orchids are probably being overwatered, and we should water them less.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the greenhouse manager's argument?
choices: Dr. Tesh has observed at least one Cassel orchid in a greenhouse that wilted because it was overwatered.
Most botanists who study orchids accept Dr. Tesh's claim about the cause of wilting in Cassel orchids.
What causes Cassel orchids to wilt in the wild is at least some indication of what causes them to wilt when grown in greenhouses.
Overwatering is a more common cause of wilting among greenhouse plants than among plants that grow wild.
Reducing the amount of water the greenhouse's Cassel orchids receive will not cause them any harm.
questions.explanation: Tesh's authority comes entirely from studying wild orchids, so the manager must assume her knowledge carries over at least somewhat to greenhouse orchids; if wild wilting tells us nothing about greenhouse wilting, her say-so is irrelevant. C states this modestly. A is the tempting trap because it would make Tesh more qualified, but her expertise can transfer even if she has never seen a greenhouse case herself.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The greenhouse orchids are probably overwatered, so they should be watered less.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dr. Tesh, who has studied wild Cassel orchids for thirty years, says wilting in Cassel orchids almost always comes from too much water; no one knows them better.

breakdown.analysis: Tesh is an expert on Cassel orchids, but only on wild ones in cloud forests. A greenhouse is a different place: different light, soil, pots, humidity. So what does a field expert's rule tell us about a potted plant? The manager needs her wild-orchid knowledge to say at least something about greenhouse orchids. If it doesn't, her authority is out of its range, like trusting a marine biologist who studies wild salmon to diagnose your aquarium goldfish. Prephrase: Tesh's knowledge of wild orchids applies, at least somewhat, to greenhouse ones.

choices.note: Tempting, because it would shore up Tesh's credentials for this exact setting. But it isn't required. Negate it: she's never seen a greenhouse case. Her general knowledge of the plant could still carry over. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Dr. Tesh has never observed a Cassel orchid in a greenhouse that wilted because it was overwatered.

choices.note: Not needed. The manager relies on Tesh being the top expert, not on a consensus. Negate it and the argument is a bit less comfortable, but its logic is untouched.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most botanists who study orchids accept Dr. Tesh's claim about the cause of wilting in Cassel orchids.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: wild wilting gives no indication at all of greenhouse wilting. Then Tesh's thirty years in the cloud forest tell us nothing about these orchids, and the argument has no support left. Note the modest wording ('at least some indication'). Required assumptions are often this weak.
choices.negation: What causes Cassel orchids to wilt in the wild gives no indication at all of what causes them to wilt when grown in greenhouses.

choices.note: An unneeded comparison. The argument is about Cassel orchids specifically and doesn't need any ranking of greenhouse vs. wild plants in general. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: Overwatering is not a more common cause of wilting among greenhouse plants than among plants that grow wild.

choices.note: Too strong. The manager can recommend less water even if cutting back carries some small risk. Negate it (some harm is possible) and the recommendation still makes sense if overwatering is the likely cause.
choices.negation: Reducing the amount of water the greenhouse's Cassel orchids receive will cause them at least some harm.

questions.stimulus: Labor economist Rhea Dalton argues that the province's proposed ban on noncompete agreements would raise wages for warehouse workers, because employers would have to compete harder to keep them. But Dalton has spent most of her career as a paid consultant to labor unions, which have long campaigned for such a ban. Her argument should therefore be rejected.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: rejects an argument on the basis of the circumstances of the person who advances it rather than on its merits
presumes, without providing justification, that the proposed ban would not raise wages for warehouse workers
relies on the testimony of an economist about a matter that lies outside her area of expertise
fails to consider that some employers might benefit from a ban on noncompete agreements
draws a conclusion about all workers in the province from evidence concerning only warehouse workers
questions.explanation: Ad hominem: Dalton gives a reason (employers would have to compete to keep workers), but the argument ignores that reason and rejects her case because she has worked for unions. A describes this. B is the tempting trap, but the argument concludes only that Dalton's argument should be rejected; it never asserts that wages would not rise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dalton's argument that the noncompete ban would raise warehouse wages should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dalton has long been a paid consultant to unions, which support the ban.

breakdown.analysis: Dalton gave a real reason: without noncompetes, employers have to compete to keep workers. Did the arguer say anything about that reason? No. It just points at who has paid her. Her ties to unions might be a reason to check her work carefully, but they don't make her reasoning wrong. This is the ad hominem (circumstantial) flaw. Know it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument rejects Dalton's case because of her union consulting work, never engaging her actual reason about employers competing for workers.
Tempting, but the argument stops at 'reject her argument.' It never claims wages won't rise. Rejecting someone's argument isn't the same as asserting the opposite.
Dalton is a labor economist talking about wages. That's squarely her field. No inappropriate authority here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous tenor says the ban will raise wages, so it will.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether some employers benefit has nothing to do with the move from Dalton's background to rejecting her argument.
The argument only discusses warehouse workers. It doesn't generalize to all workers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Warehouse wages rose after the ban, so every worker's wages will rise.

questions.stimulus: Software manager: Kwame has proposed that our team stop requiring a second reviewer for small code changes, arguing that such reviews delay releases more than they improve quality. But Kwame is the team member who has most often been criticized for submitting careless code. So his proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the software manager's argument?
choices: Second reviews of small code changes improve code quality more than they delay releases.
No other member of the team supports Kwame's proposal.
Kwame made his proposal primarily in order to avoid criticism of his own code.
Team members who have been criticized for careless code produce more errors than any other team members.
Kwame's history of submitting careless code is at least some reason to doubt the merits of his proposal.
questions.explanation: The manager rejects the proposal solely because of Kwame's record, so the argument requires that his record has some bearing on whether the proposal is any good; negate E and the only reason for rejection disappears. C is the tempting trap: a self-serving motive would help the manager, but the argument can stand on Kwame's record without any claim about why he made the proposal.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kwame's proposal to drop second reviews for small changes should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kwame is the team member most often criticized for careless code.

breakdown.analysis: Kwame offered a reason: small-change reviews cost more time than they're worth. The manager ignores it and points to Kwame's track record. For that to count as a reason to reject the proposal, the manager has to assume that who Kwame is tells us something about whether his idea is good. That's the hidden premise in every ad hominem. Prephrase: Kwame's record bears on the merits of his proposal.

choices.note: Tempting, since it supports the conclusion. But the manager's argument doesn't rest on any claim about what reviews actually do. Negate it (reviews don't improve quality more than they delay) and the manager's reasoning, which is all about Kwame, isn't touched.
choices.negation: Second reviews of small code changes do not improve code quality more than they delay releases.

choices.note: Not required. Others could agree with Kwame and the manager could still reject the idea on the stated grounds. Negate it and nothing breaks.
choices.negation: At least one other member of the team supports Kwame's proposal.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like what the manager is hinting at. But the argument never mentions motives; it relies on his record. Negate it (avoiding criticism wasn't his main reason) and the manager can still lean on the record.
choices.negation: Kwame did not make his proposal primarily in order to avoid criticism of his own code.

choices.note: Too strong ('more than any other'). The argument doesn't need a ranking of error rates. Negate it and the reasoning is unaffected.
choices.negation: Team members who have been criticized for careless code do not produce more errors than all other team members.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Kwame's record gives no reason at all to doubt his proposal. Then the manager's only reason for rejecting it is gone. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Kwame's history of submitting careless code gives no reason at all to doubt the merits of his proposal.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Several scholars have argued that the Varrian inscriptions, which celebrate the victories of King Osric, were carved centuries after his reign. But every one of these scholars trained at Delmont University, whose faculty has long been hostile to work that glorifies Osric. So their dating should be disregarded, and the inscriptions most likely date from Osric's own reign.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?
choices: Some scholars who did not train at Delmont University doubt that the inscriptions accurately describe Osric's victories.
The scholars' dating rests on letter forms that occur in no other surviving text from Osric's reign but are common in texts from two centuries later.
Delmont University's faculty has published studies praising several rulers who lived before Osric.
Inscriptions celebrating a king's victories were usually carved while that king was still alive.
The historian has written a popular book that portrays Osric's reign in an extremely favorable light.
questions.explanation: The historian dismisses the late dating by pointing to the scholars' training and supposed bias, never to their evidence. B gives independent evidence for the late dating that stands regardless of anyone's motives, exposing the ad hominem. A is the tempting trap because it shows that critics exist outside Delmont, but those critics doubt the inscriptions' accuracy, not their date; E is a tu quoque against the historian, which no more refutes the argument than the historian's attack refutes the scholars.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scholars' late dating should be disregarded; the inscriptions most likely date from Osric's reign.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All the late-dating scholars trained at Delmont, whose faculty is hostile to work glorifying Osric.

breakdown.analysis: The historian never looks at the scholars' evidence. It just says: consider where they trained. Even if Delmont people dislike Osric, that doesn't make their dating wrong. Biased people can be right. So what weakens this? Show that the late dating has solid support that doesn't depend on anyone's attitude toward Osric. Then the historian's attack misses entirely.

choices.note: Tempting. It seems to show the doubters aren't all Delmont people. But read closely: these scholars doubt the inscriptions' accuracy, not their date. The dating question is untouched.

CORRECT. Here's evidence for the late date that has nothing to do with bias: the letter forms match texts from two centuries later, not Osric's time. That makes the dating credible whoever proposed it, so dismissing it on the basis of the scholars' training fails.
So? Praising earlier rulers doesn't show Delmont is fair to Osric, and even if it did, it wouldn't give positive evidence about the date.
This strengthens the historian. If such inscriptions were usually carved during the king's life, an early date looks more likely.
Tempting as a 'gotcha,' but it's an ad hominem against the historian. The historian's possible bias doesn't make the conclusion false, just as the scholars' possible bias doesn't make theirs false.
choices.example: Example of flaw: You can't trust her defense of Osric; she wrote a book praising him.

questions.stimulus: Station manager: Corbin, our weather forecaster, claims that the station's new radar software regularly misreports rainfall totals. But Corbin was passed over for promotion to chief meteorologist shortly after the software was installed, and he has resented the station's management ever since. Therefore, his claim about the software is false.
questions.stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the station manager's argument?
choices: Garza claims that the old footbridge in Wilton Park needs repair. But Garza is a schoolteacher, not an engineer. So we have no good reason to believe that the footbridge needs repair.
Ines says that the new vaccine is safe, and Ines works for the company that makes it. But Ines bases her claim on independent trials. So her claim is probably true.
Pratt maintains that Selwyn's new novel is overrated. But Pratt has disliked all of Selwyn's earlier novels. So Pratt's opinion of the new novel probably reflects that long-standing dislike.
Hollis contends that the county's new zoning code is unconstitutional. But Hollis owns land whose value was reduced when the code took effect. Therefore, the zoning code is constitutional.
Ruiz argues that the city should build a new park downtown. But proposals for downtown parks have failed several times in the past. Therefore, Ruiz's proposal will fail.
questions.explanation: The manager concludes that Corbin's claim is false because Corbin has a personal grievance, an ad hominem that moves from a person's motive to the falsity of what he says. D matches exactly: Hollis's financial stake is taken to show the code is constitutional. C is the tempting trap because it also cites a critic's personal history, but it concludes only something about where Pratt's opinion comes from, which is reasonable, not that his claim is false.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corbin's claim that the radar software misreports rainfall is false.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corbin was passed over for promotion after the software arrived and resents management.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Person X claims P; X has a personal motive or grievance related to P; therefore P is false.

breakdown.analysis: Corbin's grudge might make you double-check his claim. It doesn't show the software works. Plenty of resentful people are right. The flaw: a person's motive is used to conclude that his claim is false. Two pieces must match: 1. the evidence is about the claimant's personal circumstances or motive; 2. the conclusion is that the claim itself is false (not just doubtful).

choices.note: Close in feel, but this attacks Garza's qualifications, not her motives, and it concludes only that we lack good reason to believe her, a much weaker conclusion than 'the claim is false.'
No flaw here. It acknowledges a possible bias and then points to independent evidence. That's reasonable.

Tempting: a critic with a personal history against the target. But the conclusion is only that Pratt's opinion likely reflects his dislike, which follows fairly well. It never says 'so the novel isn't overrated.'
CORRECT. Hollis has a personal stake (his land lost value), and that's used to conclude his claim is false (the code is constitutional). Motive → claim false, just like Corbin.
This predicts failure from past failures, an argument from track record, not an attack on Ruiz's motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The last three bond measures lost, so this one will too.

questions.stimulus: Several vintners in the Osterlund region have endorsed winemaker Jonas Ferrier's recommendation that vines in the region not be irrigated, accepting his claim that irrigation dilutes the flavor of the grapes. But Ferrier's own vineyard has been irrigated every summer for the past decade. Osterlund's vintners should therefore disregard his recommendation and keep irrigating their vines.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument's reasoning?
choices: It relies on the judgment of an authority whose expertise lies outside the matter at issue.
It fails to consider that irrigation might affect qualities of the grapes other than their flavor.
It regards a fact about the advocate of a position as showing that the reasons offered for that position are inadequate.
It presumes, without providing justification, that what holds for Ferrier's vineyard holds for every vineyard in the region.
It takes for granted that the vintners who endorsed the recommendation did so solely because of Ferrier's reputation.
questions.explanation: This is the tu quoque form of ad hominem: Ferrier gave a reason (irrigation dilutes flavor), and the argument dismisses it because Ferrier himself irrigates, a fact about him rather than about his reason. C states this abstractly. D is the most tempting trap, since vineyards differ, but the argument never uses Ferrier's vineyard as evidence about other vineyards; it uses his conduct only to discredit him.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Osterlund vintners should disregard Ferrier's recommendation and keep irrigating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ferrier recommends not irrigating because irrigation dilutes flavor, but his own vineyard is irrigated every summer.

breakdown.analysis: So Ferrier irrigates. Does that tell us whether irrigation dilutes flavor? Not at all. He could be a hypocrite, or have reasons we don't know, and his claim could still be exactly right. It's like ignoring a doctor who tells you to quit smoking because she smokes. This is the 'you too' (tu quoque) version of ad hominem. It's a classic; know it. The abstract wording to look for: a fact about the person is treated as defeating the reasons for their position.

choices.note: Ferrier is a winemaker talking about grapes. Nothing suggests he's out of his field. And the argument rejects his view rather than relying on it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous novelist says irrigation dilutes flavor, so it does.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The dispute is about flavor. Other qualities of the grapes don't bear on the move from Ferrier's conduct to rejecting his advice.
CORRECT. Ferrier's own irrigation is a fact about him. The argument treats it as defeating his reason (dilution of flavor), which it never addresses. That's tu quoque.

Tempting. Vineyards do differ, and that might explain why Ferrier irrigates. But the argument doesn't reason from 'Ferrier's vineyard is like this' to 'all vineyards are like this.' It uses his vineyard only to make him look inconsistent.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Irrigation hasn't hurt the flavor at Ferrier's vineyard, so it won't hurt the flavor anywhere in the region.

choices.note: The argument says nothing about why the vintners endorsed him. It says they accepted his claim about dilution, which is the opposite of 'solely because of his reputation.'

questions.stimulus: Gardener: The new Halvard fertilizer has become popular because it makes flowering plants bloom earlier. But it contains a compound that can stunt root growth in young ferns. This spring, the botanical garden's staff treated all of its fern beds with Halvard. So the young ferns in the garden will have stunted roots this year.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the gardener's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: mistakes an effect of stunted root growth for its cause
fails to consider that young ferns might be harmed by compounds other than the one in Halvard
draws a conclusion about all ferns from a sample of ferns that may not be representative
presumes, without providing justification, that what is true of young ferns is also true of mature ferns
treats a result that a compound is capable of producing as a result it will inevitably produce
questions.explanation: The premise says the compound can stunt roots; the conclusion says the ferns will have stunted roots. That jump from possible to certain is the flaw, and E names it. B is the tempting trap because 'fails to consider other causes' is a common flaw, but other harmful compounds would not undercut the prediction; the problem is that this compound may not stunt these ferns at all.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The garden's young ferns will have stunted roots this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Halvard contains a compound that can stunt root growth in young ferns; the fern beds were treated with Halvard.

breakdown.analysis: 'Can' isn't 'will.' Lots of things can harm you without actually doing so: the dose may be too small, the conditions may be wrong, the ferns may tolerate it. The gardener turns a possibility into a certainty. Watch for this switch between 'can/may' in a premise and 'will/must' in a conclusion. We need an answer that says the argument treats a possible effect as a sure one.

choices.note: No reversal here. The argument says the compound causes stunting, not that stunting causes something else.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ferns with stunted roots get less water, so lack of water must be what stunts their roots.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'ignores other causes' is a classic flaw. But other compounds would only make stunting more likely. The real problem is that this compound might not stunt these ferns at all.
The conclusion is about the ferns in this garden, the very ferns that were treated. No sample is being generalized.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The ferns in one bed were stunted, so every fern in the region will be.

choices.note: The argument never mentions mature ferns. Its conclusion is about young ferns only.
CORRECT. The compound can stunt roots; the gardener concludes it will. That's possibility treated as certainty.

questions.stimulus: Union representative: Under our new contract, if the plant's monthly orders fall below 40,000 units for two consecutive months, the plant's night shift will be eliminated. Orders fell below 40,000 units last month, and the company's own forecasts show that they could do so again this month. So the night shift will certainly be eliminated.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the union representative's argument?
choices: The company's forecasts that show orders could fall below 40,000 units this month also show that orders are far more likely to exceed 45,000 units.
Under the contract, workers whose shift is eliminated must be offered positions on the plant's remaining shifts.
Orders at the plant fell below 40,000 units in several months before the new contract took effect.
The contract also permits the company to eliminate the night shift for reasons unrelated to the volume of orders.
The company's forecasts of monthly orders have occasionally been less accurate than the forecasts of independent analysts.
questions.explanation: The contract's condition is sufficient for eliminating the shift, so the shift goes if orders fall short again; but the forecasts say only that this could happen, and the representative concludes it certainly will. A shows the shortfall is unlikely, which directly undercuts the certainty. E is the tempting trap, but occasional inaccuracy cuts both ways and does not make a second shortfall any less likely.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The night shift will certainly be eliminated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Below 40,000 for two straight months → night shift eliminated; below 40,000 last month; forecasts say orders could fall below 40,000 this month.

breakdown.analysis: The rule: two months in a row under 40,000 → shift eliminated. One month is done. The second month is only a 'could.' So the conclusion 'certainly' depends on something that's merely possible. What weakens this? Anything showing that a second bad month is unlikely. Then the sufficient condition probably won't be met, and the certainty evaporates.

choices.note: CORRECT. The same forecasts that show a shortfall is possible show it's unlikely; orders will probably top 45,000. Then the second bad month probably won't happen, and 'certainly eliminated' is badly overstated.
So? This is about what happens to workers after the shift is gone. It doesn't affect whether the shift is eliminated.
Irrelevant. Shortfalls before the contract don't count toward its two-month trigger, and they say little about this month.
Opposite direction. More ways to eliminate the shift makes elimination more likely, if anything.
Tempting, because it casts doubt on the forecasts. But 'occasionally less accurate' doesn't say which way they err. It doesn't make a shortfall any less likely, so it doesn't attack the certainty.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacologist: The antibiotic Corvilex is effective against most common respiratory infections, but it can cause dizziness in patients who are also taking medication for high blood pressure. Mr. Alvar has just been prescribed Corvilex, and he takes medication for high blood pressure. Therefore, Mr. Alvar will experience dizziness.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the pharmacologist's argument?
choices: Heavy rain can cause the Lund River to flood. The Lund River flooded last week. Therefore, there must have been heavy rain near the Lund River last week.
Frost kills any tomato seedling that is left uncovered overnight. The seedlings in the north bed were left uncovered last night, and there was frost. Therefore, those seedlings are dead.

A recent software update can corrupt saved files on computers that run older operating systems. The library's computers run an older operating system and received the update last night. Therefore, the library's saved files will be corrupted.
A certain pesticide kills aphids only when it is applied in warm weather. The pesticide was applied to the Ortega field during a cold spell. Therefore, the aphids in the Ortega field survived.
Dogs that are left alone for long periods often become anxious. Ms. Rook's dog is regularly left alone for long periods. Therefore, Ms. Rook's dog is probably somewhat anxious.
questions.explanation: The stimulus moves from 'X can cause Y under condition C' and 'this case meets C' to 'Y will happen,' treating a possibility as a certainty. C has exactly that structure. E is the tempting trap because its form looks similar, but it starts from 'often' and concludes only 'probably,' which is reasonable; B is valid because its premise says frost kills any uncovered seedling.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mr. Alvar will experience dizziness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corvilex can cause dizziness in patients on blood-pressure medication; Alvar takes Corvilex and blood-pressure medication.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X can cause Y when condition C holds; this case has X and C; therefore Y will occur.

breakdown.analysis: 'Can cause' means some patients in that situation get dizzy. Maybe 5 percent, maybe 50. It doesn't mean Alvar will. So the flaw is a possible effect treated as certain. To match it, look for: 1. a 'can' premise with a condition; 2. a case that meets the condition; 3. a 'will' conclusion. Watch for look-alikes that hedge ('probably') or that start from 'always' (those are valid or reasonable).

choices.note: Different flaw. This reasons backward from the effect (flood) to one possible cause (rain), ignoring other causes like snowmelt.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fever can be caused by flu. Sam has a fever. So Sam has the flu.

choices.note: Valid, not flawed. 'Kills any uncovered seedling' is a guarantee, not a possibility, so the conclusion follows.
CORRECT. The update can corrupt files on older systems; the library has older systems and the update; so the files will be corrupted. 'Can' becomes 'will,' exactly like Corvilex and Alvar.

Different structure. 'Only when warm' makes warm weather necessary for the pesticide to kill aphids, so cold weather means the pesticide didn't kill them. The flaw is concluding they survived, which ignores other things that might have killed them. No 'can' to 'will' here.
Tempting, since the shape is close. But 'often' leads only to 'probably somewhat anxious.' The conclusion is hedged to fit the premise, so it isn't flawed in the same way.

questions.stimulus: Building inspector: Termites can enter a house through any wooden structure that is in direct contact with the soil. The wooden posts that support the Pell house's back porch rest directly on the soil. So unless those posts are raised onto concrete footings, the Pell house will become infested with termites.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the building inspector's argument requires which one of the following assumptions?
choices: Raising the porch posts onto concrete footings would prevent all termite damage to the Pell house.
Termites either are already present in the soil near the Pell house or will at some point be present there.
Termites cannot enter a house except through wooden structures that are in direct contact with the soil.
The Pell house has been infested with termites at some time in the past.
Termites do more damage to porches than to any other part of a house.
questions.explanation: The premise establishes only that termites can get in through the posts; to conclude the house will be infested, the inspector must assume there are, or will be, termites around to do so. Negate B and infestation becomes impossible, so the argument collapses. C is the tempting trap, but if termites had other ways in, infestation would be more likely, not less, so the argument does not need C.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless the porch posts are raised onto concrete footings, the Pell house will become infested.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Termites can enter through any wood touching the soil; the Pell porch posts rest on the soil.

breakdown.analysis: The posts give termites a way in. But a door isn't a visitor. If there are no termites in the area, now or ever, an open path doesn't matter. The inspector moves from 'termites can get in' to 'termites will get in,' so the argument needs, at minimum, that termites will actually be around to use that path. Prephrase: there are, or will be, termites near the house. Note how modest the right answer is. It doesn't say 'many termites' or 'termites now.'

choices.note: Too strong, and not what 'unless' commits the inspector to. The claim is: posts not raised → infestation. It doesn't say raising them guarantees safety. Negate it (raising wouldn't stop all damage) and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Raising the porch posts onto concrete footings would not prevent all termite damage to the Pell house.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: there are no termites near the Pell house and there never will be. Then nothing can come through the posts, and the prediction of infestation falls apart.
choices.negation: Termites are not present in the soil near the Pell house, nor will they ever be present there.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like it makes the posts the key issue. But negate it: termites can also get in other ways. That makes infestation more likely, not less. The argument doesn't need the posts to be the only route.
choices.negation: Termites can enter a house in at least one way other than through wooden structures in direct contact with the soil.

choices.note: Not needed. A house can be infested for the first time. Negate it (never infested before) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: The Pell house has never been infested with termites.

choices.note: Irrelevant ranking. The argument is about whether infestation happens, not where termites do the most damage.
choices.negation: Termites do not do more damage to porches than to every other part of a house.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Some historians maintain that the bronze tools found at the ancient settlement of Kessa must have been imported, since no tin deposits have been found anywhere near the site. But chemical analysis shows that the tin in the tools matches that of a small deposit, discovered only last year, in hills thirty kilometers from Kessa. Thus the tools were made at Kessa, and the historians are mistaken.
questions.stem: The archaeologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: relies on a chemical analysis without establishing that the people who performed it were qualified to do so
rejects the historians' position by attacking their motives rather than by addressing their evidence
treats the absence of evidence that tin deposits existed near Kessa as proof that none existed
takes evidence that removes an obstacle to a hypothesis as sufficient to establish that the hypothesis is true
draws a conclusion about all of the bronze tools at Kessa from an analysis of only some of them
questions.explanation: The historians' reason for saying the tools were imported was that there was no nearby tin; the new deposit removes that obstacle, showing local manufacture was possible. But the archaeologist concludes the tools were made at Kessa, even though the tin could have been carried elsewhere and the tools brought back. D describes this possible-to-actual move abstractly. C is the tempting trap because an absence-of-evidence flaw is present, but it is the historians' flaw, not the archaeologist's.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Kessa tools were made at Kessa; the historians are mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The historians said 'imported' because no tin was found nearby; the tools' tin matches a newly found deposit thirty kilometers away.

breakdown.analysis: The new deposit knocks out the historians' reason. Fine. But what does it prove? That local manufacture was possible. Does it prove the tools were actually made at Kessa? No. Tin from those hills could have been carried to some other town, cast into tools there, and the tools brought to Kessa. 'Could have been made here' isn't 'was made here.' It's like proving a suspect had a key to the room and concluding he's the thief. Notice that this flaw is described abstractly here, as removing an obstacle and calling the hypothesis proven.

choices.note: Nothing suggests the analysts were unqualified, and the argument's problem isn't trust in the lab. It's what the result actually shows.
choices.example: Example of flaw: My neighbor ran the test in his garage and says the tin matches, so it does.

choices.note: The archaeologist doesn't mention the historians' motives at all. It addresses their evidence (no nearby tin) head-on.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Those historians just want to make Kessa look backward, so ignore their dating.

choices.note: Tempting, because there is an absence-of-evidence flaw in this story. But it's the historians' flaw (no deposit found, so none existed). The question asks about the archaeologist's reasoning.

CORRECT. The tin match removes the obstacle to local manufacture (no nearby tin). The archaeologist then treats the hypothesis 'made at Kessa' as established, ignoring that the tin could have been worked elsewhere.
The stimulus says the tin in the tools matches, with no hint that only some were tested. Even if it were a subset, that's not where the reasoning goes wrong.

questions.stimulus: Engineering director: We track how long each engineer takes, on average, to resolve a software defect. By that measure, each of the five engineers on our Velo team is faster than any engineer on our Arden team. Therefore, the Velo team as a whole resolves defects faster than the Arden team does, and Velo should be assigned the backlog of urgent defects.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the engineering director's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about all software engineers from a sample of only five engineers
presumes that what is true of each member of a group must also be true of the group as a whole
takes for granted that the speed at which defects are resolved is the only measure of a team's quality
confuses a condition that is necessary for resolving defects quickly with one that is sufficient
fails to consider that the Arden team's engineers may be more experienced than those on the Velo team
questions.explanation: Part-whole (composition): each Velo engineer is faster than each Arden engineer, but a team's overall output also depends on how many engineers it has and how they work together; Arden might have many more engineers. B names this. A is the tempting trap because 'five' sounds like a small sample, but the director concludes only about these two teams, not about software engineers in general.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Velo team as a whole resolves defects faster than Arden, so Velo should get the urgent backlog.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of Velo's five engineers is individually faster than any Arden engineer.

breakdown.analysis: Faster individuals don't guarantee a faster team. What if Arden has twenty engineers and Velo has five? Twenty slower people can still clear more defects than five fast ones. It's like saying every player on a three-person rowing crew is stronger than anyone on an eight-person crew, so the three-person boat is faster. This is the part-to-whole (composition) flaw. Know it.

choices.note: Tempting, because five sounds small. But the conclusion isn't about software engineers in general. It's about these two teams, and the director has data on every Velo engineer.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Five engineers I surveyed prefer tabs, so most engineers prefer tabs.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each Velo engineer is faster, so the director concludes the Velo team is faster. That moves a property of the parts to the whole without justification.
The director never claims Velo is the better team overall, only that it's faster at resolving defects. No shift to quality.
No conditional is in play. Nothing is stated as necessary or sufficient for quick resolution.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Fast teams use code review, and we use code review, so we're fast.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The director already gives speed data on each engineer; experience is just one possible reason for speed, and it doesn't touch the jump from individuals to teams.

questions.stimulus: Labor analyst: Some regional officials doubt that the Tarran region's labor market improved at all last year. They are mistaken. Last year, the unemployment rate declined in each of the four counties that make up the Tarran region. It follows that the unemployment rate for the Tarran region as a whole also declined last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the labor analyst's argument?
choices: Unemployment rates declined last year in most regions of the country.
The county with the highest unemployment rate in the Tarran region had the smallest decline in that rate last year.
Several large employers opened new facilities in the Tarran region last year.
Last year, the Tarran region's labor force grew more slowly than the labor force of the country as a whole.
The share of the Tarran region's labor force living in each of its four counties was nearly the same at the end of last year as at the beginning.
questions.explanation: A region's unemployment rate is an average of its counties' rates weighted by labor-force size, so it can rise even when every county's rate falls if workers shift toward a high-unemployment county. E rules out such a shift, closing the part-to-whole gap. C is the tempting trap because new employers sound like good news, but every county's rate already fell; the question is whether the regional figure follows, and C says nothing about that.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tarran's regional unemployment rate declined last year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The unemployment rate declined in each of Tarran's four counties.

breakdown.analysis: Seems airtight, right? It isn't. A regional rate is a weighted average. Suppose County A has 2 percent unemployment and County B has 12 percent. Both drop a point, to 1 and 11. But if lots of workers moved from A to B during the year, the region's overall rate can still go up, because more of the labor force now sits in the high-unemployment county. Rates of the parts don't fix the rate of the whole. We need something saying the mix didn't shift much.

choices.note: Other regions are irrelevant. The trend elsewhere tells us nothing about how Tarran's counties add up.
If anything, slightly worrying. It says the worst county improved the least, but it gives no information about the labor-force mix. It doesn't close the gap.

Tempting, since new jobs sound like lower unemployment. But we already know every county's rate fell. The question is whether those declines add up to a regional decline, and this says nothing about that.
Irrelevant comparison. How fast Tarran's labor force grew compared with the country's has no bearing on whether the county declines add up to a regional one.

CORRECT. If each county's share of the labor force stayed about the same, the weights in the regional average didn't change. Every county's rate fell, so the weighted average fell too. This rules out the shift that could have broken the argument.

questions.stimulus: Broadcaster: Critics charge that our three-hour Saturday morning broadcast, which mixes cartoons with news and nature segments, exposes young children to too much distressing content. But a panel of child psychologists reviewed each of the broadcast's twelve segments separately and found that none contains too much distressing content for young children. So the critics' charge is unfounded.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the broadcaster's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that because no part of a whole has a certain property, the whole cannot have that property
relies on the judgment of experts in a field that is unrelated to the question at issue
rejects the critics' charge on the basis of the critics' motives rather than their reasons
fails to consider that many people who watch the broadcast are not young children
treats the failure to find evidence that a segment is distressing as proof that it is not distressing
questions.explanation: Part-whole: 'too much' content adds up, so twelve segments that each stay under the limit can together exceed it over three hours. The broadcaster infers that the whole lacks a property because no part has it, which A describes. E is the tempting trap, but the panel made a positive finding about each segment; the problem is not the quality of that evidence but the jump from segments to the whole broadcast.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics' charge that the broadcast exposes children to too much distressing content is unfounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Child psychologists reviewed each of twelve segments separately and found none contains too much distressing content.

breakdown.analysis: 'Too much' adds up. One scary segment might be fine. Twelve mildly scary segments in a row might not be. It's like saying no single cookie has too much sugar, so a box of twelve doesn't either. The critics' charge is about the whole three-hour broadcast; the panel looked only at pieces. You might think the problem is trusting the psychologists. It isn't. They're the right experts. The problem is the move from parts to whole.

choices.note: CORRECT. No segment has too much distressing content, so the broadcaster concludes the whole broadcast doesn't. But amounts accumulate, so the whole can have a property none of its parts has.
Child psychologists judging what distresses young children is right in their field. No inappropriate authority.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous chef says the broadcast is fine for children, so it is.

choices.note: The broadcaster never mentions the critics' motives. It responds with evidence, just the wrong kind.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics run a rival station, so ignore their complaint.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The charge is specifically about young children, so other viewers don't matter.
Tempting. But the panel didn't just fail to find a problem. It reviewed each segment and found none had too much. That's positive evidence about the parts. The flaw is applying it to the whole.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the show upsets children, so it doesn't.

questions.stimulus: Builder: Our firm wants its new model home to qualify for the state's top energy-efficiency rating. Every component we plan to install in the home, including the windows, the wall panels, the roofing, and the furnace, individually carries the state's top efficiency rating for its category. So once the home is built, it will qualify for the top rating.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the builder's argument?
choices: Homes built entirely from top-rated components generally cost more to build than other homes of the same size.
Some homes that the firm built in the past failed to qualify for the state's top energy-efficiency rating.
The state's top efficiency rating for windows is easier to obtain than its top rating for furnaces.
The state's rating for a completed home is based largely on air leakage where components meet, which is not measured when individual components are rated.
Few homebuyers in the state consider energy-efficiency ratings when deciding which home to buy.
questions.explanation: The builder assumes that because every component is top rated, the whole home will be. D shows that the home's rating depends largely on something no component rating captures, leakage at the joints, so top-rated parts do not ensure a top-rated whole. B is the tempting trap, but nothing indicates those earlier homes used top-rated components, so their failure says nothing about this plan.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The finished model home will qualify for the state's top energy-efficiency rating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every component (windows, wall panels, roofing, furnace) is individually top rated.

breakdown.analysis: Great parts, so a great whole? Not necessarily. A house loses heat through the gaps between components as well as through the components themselves. If the whole-house rating looks at something the component ratings ignore, top-rated parts won't guarantee a top-rated home. It's like assuming a band of all-star soloists must sound great together. We want an answer showing the whole is judged on something the parts' ratings don't capture.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The goal is the rating, not the cost. An expensive home can still qualify.
Tempting, since it hints the firm has failed before. But we don't know those homes used top-rated components. Without that, their failure tells us nothing about this plan.
Irrelevant comparison. How hard each component rating is to earn doesn't matter; the builder already has the top rating in every category.

CORRECT. The home's rating depends mostly on leakage at the joints, which no component rating measures. So the whole can fall short even if every part is top rated, exactly the gap the builder ignores.
Wrong goal. The firm wants the rating, not to sway buyers. Whether buyers care doesn't affect whether the home qualifies.

questions.stimulus: The vineyards of the Morland Valley, taken together, produce more grapes per hectare than the vineyards of any other valley in the province. The Hessel vineyard is in the Morland Valley, and the Dunmore vineyard is in the neighboring Callan Valley. Therefore, the Hessel vineyard produces more grapes per hectare than the Dunmore vineyard does.
questions.stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every physician at the Linden Clinic has more years of experience than any physician at the Rowe Clinic. Dr. Abe practices at Linden and Dr. Faro practices at Rowe. Therefore, Dr. Abe has more years of experience than Dr. Faro.
The Grafton school district spends more per student than any other district in the state. Therefore, Grafton's total spending on its schools is greater than that of any other district in the state.

Kaur, a teller at the bank's Elm Street branch, must process more transactions per hour than Lund, a teller at the Hill Road branch, since the Elm Street tellers as a group process more transactions per hour than the tellers at any other branch.

Each reporter on the Ledger's staff writes more articles per week than any reporter at the Courier. Therefore, the Ledger's staff as a whole produces more articles per week than the Courier's staff does.
Most of the novels on this year's shortlist for the Arden Prize were written by first-time authors. Kemp's novel is on the shortlist. Therefore, Kemp is probably a first-time author.
questions.explanation: The stimulus infers that a particular member of one group outperforms a particular member of another because the first group, taken together, outperforms the second (division). C does the same, though it states its conclusion first: the Elm Street tellers' group rate is used to rank one Elm Street teller above one Hill Road teller. D is the most tempting trap because it is also a part-whole flaw, but it runs in the opposite direction, from members to the group (composition).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hessel produces more grapes per hectare than Dunmore.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Morland's vineyards together outproduce every other valley's per hectare; Hessel is in Morland, Dunmore is in Callan.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Group A, taken as a whole, beats group B on a rate; a is in A and b is in B; therefore a beats b on that rate.

breakdown.analysis: A valley's per-hectare figure is an aggregate. Morland could have a few giant, high-yield estates and a handful of poor little plots, with Hessel among the poor ones. Callan could have a lower average but contain Dunmore, a standout. So the group's figure doesn't tell you where any one member falls. This is the whole-to-part (division) flaw. To match it, the answer must: 1. start from a group-level comparison; 2. conclude about individual members of each group. Watch for the reverse direction (parts to whole); it's a different flaw.

choices.note: Valid. 'Every physician at Linden beats any physician at Rowe' is a member-by-member claim, so it does guarantee Abe beats Faro. No whole-to-part leap.
Tempting, since it's statistical. But this confuses a per-student rate with a total, a percent-versus-number flaw, and it never moves from a group to an individual member.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our town has the highest crime rate in the county, so it has the most crimes.

choices.note: CORRECT. It's built backward (conclusion first), but the structure matches: Elm Street's tellers as a group have the higher rate, so one Elm Street teller beats one Hill Road teller. Group figure → individual comparison.
Very tempting, because it's also a part-whole flaw. But it goes the other way: from each member to the group as a whole (composition). The stimulus goes from the group to a member (division).
choices.example: Example of the stimulus's direction instead: The Ledger's staff as a whole writes the most articles, so each Ledger reporter writes more than each Courier reporter.

choices.note: Reasonable, not flawed. 'Most' supports 'probably,' and the conclusion is hedged to match.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Lack of Evidence, Sampling, Analogy, Overreaching

questions.stimulus: Oceanographer: Thirty years ago, recreational divers regularly reported seeing the comb jelly Lucerna vitrea in the waters off Cape Moray. Last spring, our research vessel spent six weeks towing fine-mesh plankton nets throughout those waters, and not one of our hundreds of hauls contained a specimen of Lucerna vitrea. Clearly, this species no longer lives off Cape Moray.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the oceanographer's argument?
choices: Average water temperatures off Cape Moray have risen noticeably over the past thirty years.
Comb jellies such as Lucerna vitrea are so fragile that towed nets almost always reduce them to unidentifiable fragments.
Most of the divers who reported seeing Lucerna vitrea thirty years ago were amateurs rather than trained marine biologists.
Lucerna vitrea is still commonly seen in waters several hundred kilometers south of Cape Moray.
The plankton nets used last spring captured large numbers of small crustaceans and fish larvae.
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the oceanographer treats the nets' failure to turn up Lucerna vitrea as proof that the species is gone. B shows that towed nets would not yield a recognizable specimen even if the jelly were plentiful, so the empty hauls prove little. C is the tempting trap, but casting doubt on the old sightings does nothing to show the jelly is there now; D concerns a different location.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lucerna vitrea no longer lives off Cape Moray.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Divers reported it thirty years ago; six weeks of net hauls last spring caught no specimen.

breakdown.analysis: So the nets came up empty. Would the nets have caught this animal if it were there? If not, the empty hauls mean nothing. Not finding something is only evidence it's absent when your search could have found it. It's like checking for termites by looking for them in the mail: no termites in the mailbox doesn't mean the house is clean. We need an answer that says the nets were a bad way to detect this jelly.

choices.note: Warmer water gives a reason the jelly might have died off. If anything, this helps the conclusion.
CORRECT. If nets shred comb jellies beyond recognition, a net survey would come up empty whether or not the species is there. The silence of the hauls stops being evidence of absence.
Tempting. It attacks the old sightings, so it feels like it attacks the argument. But the conclusion is that the jelly isn't there now. Doubting that it was ever there doesn't show it's there today.
Wrong place. The conclusion is only about Cape Moray. Thriving hundreds of kilometers away says nothing about whether it lives off the cape.
This shows the nets do catch small animals, which makes the survey look competent. That helps the argument, not hurts it.

questions.stimulus: Folklorist: Some scholars maintain that the legend of the drowned bell of Carrow was first told in inland farming villages and only later spread to the fishing towns on the coast. Yet in more than a century of collecting, folklorists have not recorded a single inland version of the legend that is older than the earliest coastal versions. So the legend must have originated in the coastal fishing towns.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the folklorist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on the work of collectors without establishing that they are authorities on the legend's history
presumes that a legend told in two different kinds of communities must carry the same meaning in each
attempts to discredit the scholars' position by questioning their motives rather than their evidence
treats the lack of evidence for one account of the legend's origin as establishing that a rival account is true
takes for granted that a view held by most folklorists is more likely than not to be correct
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the folklorist moves from 'no old inland version has been recorded' to 'the legend began on the coast.' D names that leap; an inland oral tradition could be old without ever having been written down. A is the tempting trap because the argument does cite collectors, but it uses their records as data, not their opinions as authority.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Carrow bell legend originated in the coastal fishing towns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some scholars say it began inland; but no recorded inland version is older than the earliest coastal versions.

breakdown.analysis: So nobody wrote down an old inland version. Does that mean there wasn't one? Farming villages telling stories around the fire don't leave paper trails. The folklorist takes the scholars' lack of proof and treats it as proof of the opposite view. That's absence of evidence, a classic worth knowing. It's like saying: you can't prove you were home last night, so you must have been at the party. We need an answer that says lack of support for one view was treated as proof of the other.

choices.note: Tempting, since the argument leans on a century of collecting. But it uses the collectors' records as data, not their opinions as authority. The problem isn't who collected; it's what the silence of the records can prove.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dr. Vance, a celebrated surgeon, says the bridge is structurally sound, so it must be.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument says nothing about what the legend means in each place.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The bell legend is told inland and on the coast, so it must symbolize the same loss in both.

choices.note: The folklorist never mentions the scholars' motives. No personal attack here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The scholars only say it began inland because they are from inland families, so they're wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. No recorded early inland version is a lack of evidence for the scholars' account. The folklorist treats it as establishing the coastal account, even though an old inland tradition might simply never have been written down.
The argument never appeals to what most folklorists believe. It appeals to what they have recorded.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most folklorists think the legend is coastal, so it probably is.

questions.stimulus: Mining consultant: For decades, prospectors who have worked the hills above Dunmere have claimed that the hills contain a rich vein of silver. But not one of these prospectors has ever produced an assay report confirming that claim. So there is no rich vein of silver in the hills above Dunmere.
questions.stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in the mining consultant's argument is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Several residents have long said that the old Wexley bridge was built by convict laborers. But no one has ever found a document confirming this. So the Wexley bridge was not built by convict laborers.
Several residents have long said that the old Wexley bridge is unsafe. But no one has ever found evidence that the bridge is safe. So the Wexley bridge is unsafe.
Every geologist who has studied the Kelso basin believes it holds natural gas. Since these geologists are the leading experts on the region, the basin must hold natural gas.
Three of the wells recently drilled near Ashby struck fresh water. So nearly every well drilled anywhere in the county will strike fresh water.
If a cave is home to a bat colony, its floor will be covered with guano. The floor of Orrin Cave is covered with guano. So Orrin Cave is home to a bat colony.
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the consultant concludes a claim is false merely because no one has confirmed it. A has the same shape: a claim, no confirming document, so the claim is false. B is the tempting trap; it also leans on a lack of evidence, but it runs the other way, concluding that the claim is true because its opposite hasn't been shown.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: There is no rich silver vein in the hills above Dunmere.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Prospectors claim there is one; none has produced an assay confirming it.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: People claim X; no one has confirmed X; so X is false.

breakdown.analysis: So the prospectors never got an assay. Does that show there's no silver? Maybe they never found the vein, never paid for an assay, or kept quiet to protect a claim. Unconfirmed isn't the same as false. That's absence of evidence. Match the exact shape: claim made, claim not confirmed, conclusion that the claim is false.

choices.note: CORRECT. Claim (convict labor), no confirming document, conclusion that the claim is false. Same leap from 'not confirmed' to 'false.'

Tempting. It also leans on missing evidence. But it concludes the claim is TRUE because its opposite hasn't been shown. The consultant concluded a claim is FALSE because it hasn't been confirmed. Same family, opposite direction.
choices.example: This is lack of disproof treated as proof: no one has shown the bridge is safe, so it's unsafe.

choices.note: Different flaw: appeal to authority. The experts believe it, so it's true. Nothing about missing evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The top three economists predict a recession, so a recession will happen.

choices.note: Different flaw: hasty generalization from three wells to nearly every well in the county.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The two restaurants I tried in Ostend were great, so all its restaurants are great.

choices.note: Different flaw: affirming the consequent. Bats → guano doesn't mean guano → bats.
choices.example: Example of flaw: If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. So it rained.

questions.stimulus: Epidemiologists have determined that a recent outbreak of intestinal illness in the town of Pellam was caused by the bacterium Kesselia aquatilis. Two weeks after the first cases were reported, health officials collected water samples from each of the twelve wells that supply the town. None of the samples contained Kesselia aquatilis. The officials concluded that the outbreak did not result from contamination of the town's wells.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the officials' argument depends?
choices: None of Pellam's residents who drink only bottled water became ill during the outbreak.
The water samples were tested using the most sensitive method available for detecting Kesselia aquatilis.
Kesselia aquatilis cannot be passed directly from one person to another.
No earlier outbreak of intestinal illness in Pellam has ever been traced to the town's wells.
Any well contamination by Kesselia aquatilis that caused the outbreak would not have entirely cleared within two weeks.
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: clean samples two weeks later count as proof of clean wells only if contamination would still have been detectable by then. E states that requirement; negate it and the negative tests prove nothing. B is the tempting trap, but the argument needs only an adequate test, not the most sensitive one available.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The outbreak did not result from contamination of Pellam's wells.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The outbreak was caused by Kesselia aquatilis; samples from all twelve wells, taken two weeks after the first cases, contained none.

breakdown.analysis: The samples were clean two weeks later. So what? If the bacteria flushed out of the wells in a week, a clean test at two weeks tells you nothing about what people drank. It's like checking for a gas leak two weeks after the windows were opened. The officials must assume the contamination, if there was any, would still have shown up when they tested. Prephrase: the bacteria wouldn't have disappeared from the wells before sampling.

choices.note: Not required. Negate it: some bottled-water drinkers got sick. That, if anything, fits the officials' view that the wells weren't the source. Negating doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Some of Pellam's residents who drink only bottled water became ill during the outbreak.

choices.note: Tempting, because the test's accuracy matters. But too strong. The test only has to be good enough to catch the bacterium, not the best available. Negated, a more sensitive method existed, and the argument still stands.
choices.negation: A method more sensitive than the one used was available for detecting Kesselia aquatilis.

choices.note: Not required. Person-to-person spread doesn't tell us whether the wells started the outbreak. Negate it and the argument is unaffected.
choices.negation: Kesselia aquatilis can be passed directly from one person to another.

choices.note: Irrelevant history. Whether past outbreaks came from the wells says nothing about this one. Negating changes nothing.
choices.negation: At least one earlier outbreak of intestinal illness in Pellam was traced to the town's wells.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the contamination could have completely cleared within two weeks. Then the clean samples are exactly what we'd expect even if the wells caused the outbreak, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Well contamination by Kesselia aquatilis that caused the outbreak could have entirely cleared within two weeks.

questions.stimulus: Traffic engineer: Residents of Holloway Street claim that the bicycle lane added last year is responsible for the rise in rear-end collisions on the street since then. But the police reports filed for every one of those collisions identify the factors that contributed to each crash, such as following too closely, driver distraction, and wet pavement, and not one of the reports mentions the bicycle lane. Therefore, the bicycle lane did not contribute to the rise in collisions.
questions.stem: The traffic engineer's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: rejects the residents' claim solely on the grounds that residents lack expertise in traffic safety
takes for granted that the fact that two events occurred together shows that one caused the other
presumes, without justification, that any contributor to an outcome would have been noted by those who recorded that outcome
fails to consider that collisions on Holloway Street might have increased even if the bicycle lane had not been added
concludes that the bicycle lane is safe for cyclists from evidence concerning only collisions between motor vehicles
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the reports' silence about the lane is treated as proof that the lane played no role, but reports that list driver behaviors might never record a street-design factor, such as a narrowed lane that leads drivers to follow more closely. C names that unsupported presumption. B is the attractive trap: it describes the residents' reasoning, not the engineer's, who denies a causal link rather than inferring one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bicycle lane did not contribute to the rise in rear-end collisions.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Police reports list the contributing factors for every collision; none mentions the bicycle lane.

breakdown.analysis: The reports never mention the lane. But would they? Police reports list what drivers did: following too closely, distraction. A lane that narrows the road might be exactly WHY drivers end up following too closely, and no officer would write 'bicycle lane' in the box. The engineer assumes that if the lane mattered, the reports would say so. That's absence of evidence dressed up as thorough records. It's like saying stress didn't cause your headaches because your doctor's notes only list 'tension headache.' We need an answer that says the argument assumes the records would capture the lane's role.

choices.note: The engineer never mentions the residents' expertise. The rebuttal is about the reports, not the people.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Residents aren't engineers, so their complaint about the lane can be dismissed.

choices.note: Tempting, because the topic is cause and effect. But that's the residents' reasoning (lane appeared, collisions rose). The engineer does the opposite: denies a causal link. This answer describes the wrong speaker.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions rose after the lane was added, so the lane caused them.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument only works if a contributing factor would show up in the reports. Reports that list driver behaviors may never name a design feature, even one that causes those behaviors.
So? If collisions would have risen anyway, that supports the engineer's conclusion. A 'flaw' that would help the argument isn't a flaw.
The engineer never concludes anything about cyclists' safety. The conclusion is only about the rise in collisions.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No cars have crashed in the lane, so the lane is safe for cyclists.

questions.stimulus: Veterinarian: Of the 400 cats our clinic examined during routine annual checkups last year, 35 percent were overweight. Our clinic is the largest in Corvale, and its clients come from every neighborhood in the city, rich and poor alike. So roughly a third of all the pet cats in Corvale are overweight.
questions.stem: The veterinarian's argument is flawed in that it
choices: fails to consider that cats brought in for annual checkups may differ in weight from other pet cats
confuses the percentage of examined cats that were overweight with the number of overweight cats in Corvale
takes for granted that being overweight is harmful to a cat's health
relies on the clinic's size as evidence of the competence of its veterinarians
draws a conclusion about the clinic's future clients from data about its past clients
questions.explanation: Sampling: the sample is cats brought in for routine annual checkups, but the conclusion covers all pet cats in Corvale. A points out that cats whose owners schedule yearly checkups may differ from the rest, and the clinic's citywide reach does nothing to fix that. B is the tempting trap because there are numbers, but the argument concludes about a proportion, not a count.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Roughly a third of all pet cats in Corvale are overweight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 35% of the 400 cats examined at the clinic's annual checkups were overweight; the clinic is the city's largest and draws from every neighborhood.

breakdown.analysis: Who brings a cat in for an annual checkup? Owners who are attentive enough to schedule one. Their cats could be fed differently, be older, or be indoor cats. Coverage of every neighborhood fixes geography, not the type of owner. It's like surveying gym members about exercise and calling the result 'the city's habits.' We need an answer that says the checkup cats may not represent all pet cats.

choices.note: CORRECT. The sample is cats whose owners bring them in for checkups. They may differ in weight from cats who never see a vet, so the 35% may not hold for all pet cats.
Tempting, because there are percentages. But the conclusion is a proportion ('roughly a third'), not a count. No confusion of percent and number here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: 35% of cats in Corvale are overweight but only 10% in Linden, so Corvale has more overweight cats.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about how many cats are overweight, not whether that's harmful.
The clinic's size is used to suggest a broad sample, not to vouch for its vets' skill.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ours is the biggest clinic in town, so our vets must be the best.

choices.note: The conclusion is about all pet cats in Corvale now, not the clinic's future clients.

questions.stimulus: The Larkfield Folk Dance Society mailed a questionnaire to all 400 of its members asking whether they would attend a proposed monthly evening dance. Of the 120 members who returned the questionnaire, 85 said that they would attend. On the basis of these results, the society's director concluded that a majority of the society's members would attend the monthly dance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's argument?
choices: Most residents of Larkfield who do not belong to the society have never attended a folk dance.
The questionnaire also asked members which evening of the week they would prefer for the dance.
The members who returned the questionnaire included both long-standing members and members who had joined within the past year.
Several of the members who said they would attend added that they would come only if the dance ended by ten o'clock.
Members who did not return the questionnaire have attended the society's past events about as often as those who did return it.
questions.explanation: Sampling: only 120 of 400 members answered, and people who bother to return a questionnaire may be the keenest. E strengthens by showing the non-respondents are about as engaged as the respondents, so the 85-of-120 figure is more likely to hold for the whole membership. C is the tempting trap; mixing old and new members shows variety on one dimension but says nothing about whether the respondents were unusually eager.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A majority of the society's 400 members would attend the monthly dance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 120 members returned the questionnaire, and 85 of them said they'd attend.

breakdown.analysis: Who sends back a questionnaire about a dance? The people who love dances. The 280 who didn't answer might be the ones who'd stay home. That's a self-selected sample. We need an answer that says the non-responders look like the responders in the way that matters: their interest in coming to events.

choices.note: Wrong group. Non-members' habits don't tell us what members will do.
