Irrelevant. What else the questionnaire asked doesn't make the answers more representative.
Tempting. It sounds like the respondents were a good mix. But a mix of old and new members doesn't show they weren't the most enthusiastic ones. It fixes a dimension that doesn't matter.
This casts doubt on some of the 85 yeses. If anything, it weakens.
CORRECT. The worry is that responders are keener than non-responders. If non-responders attend events just as often, the sample's yes rate is more likely to reflect the whole membership.

questions.stimulus: Loan officer: Last month we interviewed every small-business owner who had received a loan from Harwick Bank during the past year, and nearly all of them described our application process as quick and easy. Clearly, then, nearly all small-business owners who apply for a loan at Harwick Bank find the application process quick and easy.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the loan officer's argument is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: Each of the forty questions on the Ardmore aptitude exam can be answered in under a minute. So the Ardmore exam as a whole can be completed in under a minute.

A random sample of all the people who applied for a fishing license this year found that nearly all of them considered the application form clear. So nearly all applicants for fishing licenses find the form clear.

Nearly all of the hikers who reached the summit of Mount Ostrel this season and signed the summit logbook described the trail as manageable. So nearly all hikers who attempt the Ostrel trail find it manageable.
Gardeners who spread Verda mulch around their beds reported fewer weeds than gardeners who did not. So spreading Verda mulch causes gardens to have fewer weeds.
No customer of Ravel Hardware has ever filed a complaint about its return policy. So every customer of Ravel Hardware is satisfied with the return policy.
questions.explanation: Sampling: the officer surveys only applicants who succeeded (got a loan) and generalizes to everyone who applies, including those who gave up or were rejected. C does the same: it hears only from hikers who made the summit and generalizes to everyone who attempts the trail. B is the tempting trap; it matches the topic and wording, but its random sample of all applicants is representative, so its reasoning is sound.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly all small-business owners who apply to Harwick find the application process quick and easy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly all owners who received loans in the past year said so.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Surveyed only those who succeeded at X; concluded about everyone who attempts X.

breakdown.analysis: Who did they ask? Only people who got loans. What about owners who gave up halfway through the paperwork, or got rejected? They're exactly the people likely to call the process hard. This is a survivor-only sample. Find the answer that surveys only the successful and concludes about everyone who tried.

choices.note: Different flaw: part to whole. Each question is quick, so the whole exam is quick.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every brick in the wall is light, so the wall is light.

choices.note: Tempting. Same topic (applications) and nearly the same wording. But this sample is random and drawn from ALL applicants, so it's representative. Its reasoning is fine. A sound argument can't match a flawed one.
CORRECT. Only hikers who reached the top signed the logbook. Hikers who turned back, the ones most likely to find it hard, were never asked. Same survivor-only sample as the loan officer's.
Different flaw: correlation treated as causation. Mulch users have fewer weeds, so mulch causes it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Students who eat breakfast get better grades, so breakfast raises grades.

choices.note: Different flaw: treating the absence of complaints as proof of satisfaction. It's not a sample at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has told me my cooking is bad, so everyone loves it.

questions.stimulus: Last year the city of Brennock installed speed humps along Alder Lane, a residential street, as a trial. Within two months, average vehicle speeds on Alder Lane had fallen by nearly a third. The city's traffic engineer therefore argues that installing speed humps on Brennock's other residential streets would reduce average speeds on those streets by a similar proportion.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the traffic engineer's argument?
choices: After the speed humps were installed, some drivers who had regularly used Alder Lane began using nearby streets instead.
Before the trial, drivers on long, straight Alder Lane traveled much faster than drivers on most of Brennock's short, winding residential streets.
Speed humps can slightly delay fire trucks and ambulances responding to emergencies on residential streets.
Average speeds on Alder Lane fell further during the second month of the trial than during the first.
Residents of several other streets in Brennock have petitioned the city to install speed humps on their streets.
questions.explanation: Sampling: the engineer generalizes from one trial street to all residential streets. B shows Alder Lane was atypical: drivers there were much faster to begin with, so there was far more speed to cut than on the city's already slow, winding streets. A is the tempting trap, but drivers shifting to other streets concerns traffic volume, not how much humps slow the drivers who use a street.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Speed humps on Brennock's other residential streets would cut average speeds there by about a third, too.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On Alder Lane, a trial street, speeds fell by nearly a third within two months of installing humps.

breakdown.analysis: One street, then the whole city. Is Alder Lane a typical street? If drivers there were flying before the humps, there was a lot of speed to take away. On a short, winding street where people already crawl, humps can't cut speed by a third. It's like a diet that helped one heavy patient lose 30 pounds being promised to people who are already thin. We need an answer that shows the trial street differed in a way that matters.

choices.note: Tempting, because diversion is a classic problem with traffic fixes. But the conclusion is about speeds on streets that get humps, not about how many cars use them. And under the plan, the nearby streets would get humps too.

CORRECT. Alder Lane started out far faster than typical streets, so it had much more room to slow down. On streets that are already slow, the same humps probably won't cut speeds by a third. The trial street isn't representative.
Wrong dimension. This is a cost of humps, not evidence that they'd reduce speeds less. The argument is about effectiveness only.
This makes the effect look stronger and more durable. If anything, it strengthens.
Irrelevant. Residents wanting humps says nothing about how much humps would slow traffic on their streets.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, borrowers at Fenwick Credit who completed the lender's optional six-week budgeting course defaulted on their loans at a rate of 3 percent, compared with 8 percent among Fenwick's other borrowers. Fenwick's managers therefore plan to require every new borrower to complete the course, expecting that this requirement will bring the default rate among new borrowers down to about 3 percent.
questions.stem: The reasoning behind the managers' expectation is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats a reduction in the rate at which borrowers default as though it guaranteed a reduction in the total number of defaults
overlooks the possibility that running the course for every borrower would cost more than fewer defaults would save
presumes that what is true of a group of borrowers taken as a whole must be true of each borrower in that group
treats the results for a group whose members chose to join it as predictive of results for a group whose members are compelled to join
takes for granted that the default rate among Fenwick's borrowers is higher than the default rate at other lenders
questions.explanation: Sampling: the 3 percent figure comes from borrowers who volunteered for a budgeting course, and volunteers are likely more careful with money to begin with. D says, in abstract terms, that the managers project this self-selected group's results onto a group whose members will be required to take part. A is the tempting statistical trap, but the managers' expectation concerns a rate throughout, so no rate is confused with a number.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring the course for every new borrower will bring the new-borrower default rate down to about 3%.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Over five years, borrowers who took the optional course defaulted at 3%, versus 8% for other borrowers.

breakdown.analysis: Who signs up for an optional budgeting course? Borrowers who already care about their finances. They might default at 3% with or without the course. Force everyone to take it, and you add the people who'd never have chosen it, who may default just as much as before. The volunteers are a self-selected sample. It's like noting that people who voluntarily join a running club are fit, and then expecting a mandatory running club to make everyone that fit. We need an answer that says results from volunteers won't carry over to people who are made to join.

choices.note: Tempting, since there are rates everywhere. But the managers expect a lower RATE, and their evidence is about rates. Nothing is confused with a number of borrowers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our default rate fell from 8% to 3%, so we must have fewer defaults this year, even though we doubled our lending.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The managers only predict a lower default rate. Whether the course pays for itself is a different question.
Different flaw: division. The managers predict a group rate, not what each borrower will do.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Course graduates default at 3%, so Ms. Ruiz, a graduate, has a 3% chance of defaulting no matter what.

choices.note: CORRECT. The 3% comes from borrowers who chose the course. The plan applies it to borrowers who are forced to take it. Volunteers may simply be more careful with money, so their results don't predict the mandatory group's.
The argument never compares Fenwick with other lenders. Nothing here needs that assumption.

questions.stimulus: Apartment manager: Our building's lease forbids tenants to keep dogs, because barking dogs disturb the neighbors. Ferrets, like dogs, are carnivorous mammals, and many people in apartments like ours keep them as household pets. So, for the sake of consistency, the lease should also forbid tenants to keep ferrets.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the apartment manager's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that every dog kept by a tenant would disturb the neighbors
fails to consider that some tenants may wish to keep both a dog and a ferret
treats the popularity of a kind of pet as evidence that it is suitable for apartment living
draws a conclusion about all ferrets from the behavior of only a few ferrets
relies on similarities between two kinds of animals that have no bearing on the reason given for the rule
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: dogs are banned because they bark, but the manager extends the ban to ferrets on the basis of traits (being carnivorous mammals and popular pets) that have nothing to do with barking. E names this. A is the tempting trap, but the rule's rationale is a premise the manager accepts; the flaw is in the step from dogs to ferrets.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lease should also forbid ferrets.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dogs are banned because barking disturbs neighbors; ferrets, like dogs, are carnivorous mammals and popular pets.

breakdown.analysis: Why are dogs banned? Barking. Do ferrets bark? The manager never says. The similarities offered, carnivorous mammal and popular pet, have nothing to do with noise. An analogy only works if the cases share the feature that matters. It's like saying: we ban drums in the building because they're loud, and guitars, like drums, are musical instruments, so we should ban guitars. We need an answer that says the similarities are irrelevant to the reason for the rule.

choices.note: Tempting. The rule's reason does overgeneralize about dogs. But that's a premise the manager accepts, not the step being criticized. The flaw is in jumping from dogs to ferrets.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Some dogs bark at night, so every dog in the building would keep the neighbors awake.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether a tenant wants both pets has nothing to do with whether the comparison holds.
The manager mentions that ferrets are popular, but doesn't argue they're suitable because they're popular. The conclusion is that they should be banned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Lots of people keep pet pythons, so pythons are fine for apartments.

choices.note: There's no sample of ferrets here at all. The argument is about the category, not observed ferrets.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The two ferrets I've met bit me, so all ferrets bite.

choices.note: CORRECT. The rule exists because dogs bark. Being a carnivorous mammal or a popular pet has nothing to do with barking, so the shared traits don't support the same rule.

questions.stimulus: Mining company spokesperson: After we installed high-capacity ventilation fans in our Garrow mine, airborne dust levels there fell by 40 percent. Our planned Teller mine will extract the same kind of ore from rock at a similar depth. So installing the same fans at the Teller mine will reduce dust levels there by a comparable amount.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson's argument?
choices: Unlike Garrow's few long, straight tunnels, the Teller mine will have many short, branching galleries in which fan-driven air circulates poorly.
Operating the high-capacity fans costs considerably more than operating the fans they replaced at the Garrow mine.
Workers at the Teller mine will be required to wear respirators that filter out most airborne dust.
Several other mines in the region that installed the same fans also saw large reductions in their dust levels.
Ore from the Garrow mine is sold to the same smelters that are expected to buy ore from the Teller mine.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the spokesperson assumes Teller will respond like Garrow because the two mines share ore type and depth. A shows a difference that bears directly on how fans work: air does not circulate well through Teller's branching layout. C is the tempting trap; respirators protect workers, but they do nothing to the dust levels in the air, which is what the conclusion is about.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The same fans will cut dust levels at the Teller mine by about 40%.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The fans cut dust 40% at Garrow; Teller will mine the same ore at a similar depth.

breakdown.analysis: Same ore, same depth. Fine, but what makes a fan work? Moving air through the mine. If the two mines are shaped differently, the fans might not move air the same way. The analogy rests on similarities that may not be the ones that matter. We need a relevant difference: something about Teller that would make the fans less effective.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fans reduce dust by moving air. If air circulates poorly through Teller's branching galleries, the fans won't clear dust the way they did in Garrow's straight tunnels. That's a relevant difference.
Wrong dimension. Cost doesn't affect how much dust the fans remove. The conclusion is about effectiveness.
Tempting, since it's about dust and worker health. But respirators filter what workers breathe; they don't change how much dust is in the air. The conclusion is about dust levels in the mine.
More mines with good results. This strengthens the case for the fans.
Irrelevant. Who buys the ore has nothing to do with how air moves underground.

questions.stimulus: Dance company director: Two years ago the Varga Ballet stopped performing on Monday evenings, and its average ticket sales per performance rose substantially. Our company, like the Varga Ballet, performs in a city of about half a million people and stages mostly classical works. So we too should stop performing on Monday evenings, in order to increase our ticket sales per performance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its flawed reasoning to the director's argument?
choices: When Hollis Bakery stopped opening on Mondays, its weekly profits rose, because its Monday sales never covered its Monday staffing costs. Our café's Monday sales have never covered its Monday staffing costs either. So we should stop opening on Mondays to raise our weekly profits.
Three cafés on Main Street raised their prices last year and kept all of their regular customers. So any café in town could raise its prices without losing customers.
Every café on Main Street whose profits rose last year had stopped opening on Mondays. Hollis Bakery stopped opening on Mondays last year. So Hollis Bakery's profits must have risen.

When Hollis Bakery stopped opening on Mondays, its weekly profits rose. Our café, like Hollis Bakery, is located on Main Street and is known for its pastries. So we should stop opening on Mondays in order to raise our weekly profits.
Most of the shops on Main Street close on Mondays. So our café should close on Mondays as well, since following the practice of most of our neighbors is the surest way to raise our profits.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the director copies the Varga Ballet's policy on the strength of similarities (city size, repertoire) that are not shown to matter to Monday attendance. D copies Hollis Bakery's policy on the strength of shared location and pastries, which likewise are not shown to bear on Monday profits. A is the tempting trap; it uses the same policy but cites the very similarity that explains the result, so its analogy is sound.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: We should stop performing on Mondays to raise ticket sales per performance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Varga stopped Monday shows and its per-show sales rose; we, like Varga, are in a city of ~500,000 and stage mostly classical works.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Business X did A and got result R; we share some features with X (not shown to matter); so we should do A to get R.

breakdown.analysis: Why did Varga's sales per show rise? Maybe their Monday crowds were tiny, maybe they moved those patrons to weekends. The director doesn't know. City size and classical repertoire aren't shown to be what made the change work. It's like copying your neighbor's diet because you both drive Hondas. Find the argument that copies a policy based on similarities that aren't connected to why the policy worked.

choices.note: Tempting. Same policy, same structure. But this one cites the actual reason the policy worked (Monday sales didn't cover Monday costs) and shows the café shares it. That's a good analogy, not a flawed one.
Different flaw: hasty generalization from three cafés to every café in town.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Two of my friends liked the new restaurant, so everyone will like it.

choices.note: Different flaw: confusing necessary and sufficient. Closing Mondays is required for the profit rise, not a guarantee of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Everyone who passed studied; Lee studied; so Lee passed.

choices.note: CORRECT. Hollis closed Mondays and profits rose. Our café shares a street and a reputation for pastries, neither shown to matter to Monday business. So we should copy them. Same weak analogy as the director's.
Different flaw: appeal to popularity. Most neighbors do it, so we should. No comparison to one business's results.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most people in town shop at Delmar's, so it must have the best prices.

questions.stimulus: Oceanographer: Twenty years ago a warm current began shifting northward along the coast of the Brisa Gulf, and within a decade the gulf's kelp forests had largely collapsed. A warm current is now shifting northward in the same way along the Corran coast. So the kelp forests off the Corran coast will probably collapse within the next decade or so.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the oceanographer's argument?
choices: The shift of the warm current in the Brisa Gulf had no effects on marine life there other than the collapse of the kelp forests.
The kelp forests off the Corran coast are not substantially more tolerant of warm water than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests were.
The warm current off the Corran coast is shifting northward at exactly the same rate as the current in the Brisa Gulf did.
No kelp forest has ever collapsed in a region where no warm current was shifting northward.
The kelp forests off the Corran coast cover a larger area than the kelp forests of the Brisa Gulf did.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the prediction for Corran rests on Corran's being like the Brisa Gulf in the respects that matter. B rules out a relevant difference; if Corran's kelp were far more heat tolerant, the Brisa outcome would be a poor guide. C is the tempting trap, but 'exactly the same rate' is far stronger than the argument needs; a similar shift would do.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Corran's kelp forests will probably collapse within a decade or so.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A warm current's northward shift in the Brisa Gulf was followed by kelp collapse; a similar shift is happening along the Corran coast.

breakdown.analysis: Same kind of current shift, so the same result? Only if the kelp is comparable. What if Corran's kelp handles warm water far better than Brisa's did? Then the comparison falls apart. The argument needs the two cases to be alike in the way that matters. Prephrase: Corran's kelp is not much hardier against warm water than Brisa's was. Note the modest wording: the assumption is 'not substantially more tolerant,' not 'identical.'

choices.note: Not required. The current could have done other things to Brisa's marine life too. Negate it and the kelp prediction is untouched.
choices.negation: The shift of the warm current in the Brisa Gulf had at least one effect on marine life there other than the kelp collapse.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Corran's kelp is substantially more tolerant of warm water. Then the Brisa outcome tells us little about Corran, and the prediction loses its support.
choices.negation: The kelp forests off the Corran coast are substantially more tolerant of warm water than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests were.

choices.note: Tempting, because the rate of change seems relevant. But 'exactly the same' is too strong. Negated, the rates differ slightly, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: The warm current off the Corran coast is not shifting at exactly the same rate as the Brisa Gulf current did.

choices.note: Too strong and off point. Kelp could collapse for other reasons elsewhere without hurting this prediction. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one kelp forest has collapsed in a region where no warm current was shifting northward.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Size isn't tied to vulnerability here. Negate it (Corran's are not larger) and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The kelp forests off the Corran coast do not cover a larger area than the Brisa Gulf's kelp forests did.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Critics charge that short-term cash-advance loans are exploitative, noting that their fees amount to annual interest rates of several hundred percent. But a hotel room rented at $150 a night would cost nearly $55,000 if rented for a year, and no one judges a nightly room rate by what a year-long stay would cost, since hotel rooms are meant for short stays. Likewise, cash advances are meant to be repaid within a few weeks. So annualized interest rates are a misleading measure of what these loans cost borrowers.
questions.stem: The economist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that the nightly rates charged by hotels are fair to their guests
attempts to discredit the critics' position by questioning their motives for advancing it
overlooks the possibility that one of the two arrangements compared is often continued far longer than it is meant to last
treats a claim about cash-advance loans in general as though it held for each individual loan
concludes that the loans are not exploitative merely because one argument that they are has been shown to be flawed
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the hotel comparison works only if borrowers, like hotel guests, actually use the arrangement briefly. C points out that what something is meant for is not how long it is in fact used; if borrowers routinely roll advances over for months, annualized rates are not misleading. E is the tempting trap, but the economist never concludes the loans aren't exploitative, only that one measure of their cost is misleading.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Annualized interest rates are a misleading measure of what cash advances cost borrowers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A $150/night hotel room costs ~$55,000 a year, but we don't judge hotels that way because rooms are meant for short stays; cash advances are likewise meant to be repaid within weeks.

breakdown.analysis: Hotel guests really do leave after a few nights. Do borrowers really repay in a few weeks? The economist only says the loans are MEANT to be repaid quickly. If many borrowers keep rolling the loan over for months, the annual rate is exactly what they pay, and the hotel comparison breaks down. That's a flawed analogy: the cases differ on the one feature the argument relies on, how long people actually stay in. It's like saying a gym's daily pass is cheap because it's 'meant for one visit,' when most buyers come every day. We need an answer that says the loans may in practice last much longer than intended.

choices.note: Tempting, since the hotel is the economist's example. But the point isn't that hotel prices are fair; it's that annualizing a short-term price is misleading. The argument works even if hotels overcharge.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Hotels charge $150 a night, so that must be a fair price for a room.

choices.note: The economist never mentions the critics' motives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics run competing banks, so their complaint about cash advances can be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. Cash advances are meant to last weeks, but borrowers may often roll them over for months. Unlike a hotel stay, the 'short-term' use may not be real, and then the annual rate is a fair measure.
Different flaw: division. The economist talks about the loans as a type and doesn't infer anything about each individual loan.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Cash advances on average are repaid in three weeks, so Ms. Ono's will be repaid in three weeks.

choices.note: Tempting, since this flaw fits a lot of rebuttals. But read the conclusion: annualized rates are misleading. The economist never says the loans aren't exploitative.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics' math is wrong, so the loans are not exploitative.

questions.stimulus: Halden fever, a mosquito-borne illness, can be prevented in part by the use of bed nets and insect repellent. In a two-year trial, children randomly assigned to receive a new Halden fever vaccine contracted the disease at one-twentieth the rate of children randomly assigned to receive a placebo. Public health official: These results show that vaccination is the most effective way to protect children from Halden fever.
questions.stem: The public health official's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: confuses the rate at which children contracted Halden fever with the number of children who contracted it
presumes, without providing justification, that the vaccine has no harmful side effects
infers that one means of prevention is better than all others from evidence that it is far better than no prevention
relies on a comparison between groups of children who were not assigned to those groups at random
takes for granted that an illness that few children contract cannot be a serious one
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the trial compares the vaccine only with a placebo, so it shows the vaccine is effective, not that it is the most effective option. C names the jump from 'better than nothing' to 'best'; bed nets and repellent were never tested. A is the tempting trap because of the rates, but the official draws no conclusion about numbers of cases.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vaccination is the most effective way to protect children from Halden fever.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a randomized trial, vaccinated children got the disease at 1/20 the rate of placebo children; bed nets and repellent also prevent it.

breakdown.analysis: The vaccine beat a placebo. A placebo is nothing. So the vaccine beats nothing. How does it compare with bed nets or repellent? The trial never tested them. Watch the jump from 'works' to 'works best.' It's like saying a bike is the fastest way to get to work because it beats walking. We need an answer that says the evidence compares the vaccine only with no protection.

choices.note: Tempting, since numbers are flying. But the official never draws a conclusion about how many children got sick, only about which method is most effective.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The disease rate fell by half, so half as many children got sick, even though the population tripled.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Side effects matter to whether to vaccinate, but the conclusion is only about effectiveness.
CORRECT. The trial shows the vaccine is far better than a placebo, i.e., than no prevention. It says nothing about bed nets or repellent, so 'most effective' isn't supported.
Just false: the stimulus says both groups were randomly assigned. This answer is for readers who skim.
The official says nothing about how serious the illness is.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Few kids catch it, so it can't be dangerous.

questions.stimulus: Mining official: Ten years ago the Ostrava mining district adopted strict rules requiring water sprays and dust masks in all underground work. Since then, the rate at which the district's miners develop lung disease has fallen by half. Thanks to these rules, then, the district's miners now face only a low risk of lung disease.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the mining official's argument depends?
choices: The decline in the rate of lung disease among the district's miners was not due to any factor other than the dust rules.
Miners in districts that have not adopted similar rules develop lung disease at a higher rate than the district's miners now do.
No miner in the district who has complied with the dust rules has developed lung disease.
Dust is the only cause of lung disease among underground miners.
The district's miners did not formerly develop lung disease at a rate so high that even half that rate would be high.
questions.explanation: Scope shift from a relative claim (the rate fell by half) to an absolute one (the risk is now low). Halving a very high rate can still leave a high rate, so the argument requires E. A is the tempting trap, but it is too strong: the rules need only to have produced the decline, not to be its sole cause, for the official's 'thanks to these rules' to stand.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Thanks to the dust rules, the district's miners now face only a low risk of lung disease.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the rules were adopted ten years ago, the lung-disease rate has fallen by half.

breakdown.analysis: Cut in half. Is half low? If 60% of miners used to get lung disease, now it's 30%, and that's still terrible. Watch the switch from a relative word (fell by half) to an absolute one (low). It's like saying a 2,000-calorie dessert is healthy because you cut it in half. The argument needs the starting rate to have been low enough that half of it counts as low. Prephrase: the old rate wasn't so high that half is still high.

choices.note: Tempting, since it ties the drop to the rules. But too strong: 'not due to ANY other factor.' Negated, some other factor helped too, and the rules can still deserve credit. The argument survives.
choices.negation: The decline in the rate of lung disease among the district's miners was due at least partly to some factor other than the dust rules.

choices.note: Not required. Comparing with other districts doesn't tell us whether Ostrava's rate is low; all of them could be high or all low. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Miners in districts without similar rules do not develop lung disease at a higher rate than the district's miners now do.

choices.note: Way too strong. Low risk is compatible with some compliant miners getting sick. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: At least one miner in the district who has complied with the dust rules has developed lung disease.

choices.note: Too strong. Other causes (like smoking) can exist and the risk can still be low. Negating doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Dust is not the only cause of lung disease among underground miners.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the old rate was so high that half of it is still high. Then 'only a low risk' is false, and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: Before the rules were adopted, the district's miners developed lung disease at a rate so high that even half of it would still be high.

questions.stimulus: Folklore society president: Many of the region's folktales are now known only to a few elderly storytellers. Recording these storytellers on audio is one of the most effective ways to help preserve the tales they tell. Therefore, if the region's folktales are to be preserved at all, our society must fund an audio-recording program this year.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the president's argument?
choices: Only seeds stored in a cold vault remain viable for more than a few decades. Therefore, if the seed collection is to remain viable for more than a few decades, it must be stored in a cold vault.

Watering tomato plants in the evening is one of the most effective ways to help them withstand summer heat. Therefore, if a gardener's tomato plants are to withstand the summer heat, the gardener must water them in the evening.
Every heirloom apple variety that has survived to the present was grafted by orchard keepers. Therefore, any apple variety that orchard keepers graft will survive into the future.
Some of the region's tomato growers use drip irrigation, and their plants withstood last summer's heat. Therefore, all of the region's tomato growers should switch to drip irrigation.
Most professional gardeners recommend watering plants in the morning. Therefore, a gardener who wants healthy plants should water them in the morning.
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the president moves from 'recording is one of the most effective ways to help' to 'recording is required.' B makes the same move from one of the most effective ways to help tomatoes withstand heat to the only way. A is the tempting trap, but its premise already says only cold-vault storage works, so its conclusion follows validly.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the folktales are to be preserved at all, the society must fund an audio-recording program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Recording elderly storytellers is one of the most effective ways to help preserve the tales.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X is one of the best ways to help achieve G; so G requires X.

breakdown.analysis: One of the most effective ways. Not the only way. The tales could be written down, filmed, or taught to younger tellers. The president shifts from 'helps' to 'required.' It's like saying exercise is one of the best ways to lose weight, so you can't lose weight without exercise. Find the argument that turns 'one of the best ways' into 'the only way.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it ends with the same 'must' conclusion. But its premise says ONLY cold-vault seeds stay viable, so the vault really is required. That's valid; the president's isn't.
CORRECT. 'One of the most effective ways to help' becomes 'must.' Gardeners could also use shade cloth or mulch. Same shift from helpful to required.
Different flaw: confusing necessary and sufficient. Grafting was necessary for survival, not a guarantee of it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every champion trained daily; so anyone who trains daily will be a champion.

choices.note: Different flaw: generalizing from some growers to a recommendation for all, without showing irrigation made the difference.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A few students who used flashcards passed, so every student should use flashcards.

choices.note: Different flaw: appeal to authority. Experts recommend it, so do it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most chefs prefer gas stoves, so you should buy one.

questions.stimulus: Pet behaviorist: In a recent trial, owners of cats that habitually scratched furniture plugged a pheromone diffuser into an outlet in their homes. Over the following two weeks, furniture scratching in these households fell by about half compared with the two weeks before. So the diffuser offers cat owners a lasting solution to destructive scratching.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the pet behaviorist's argument?
choices: In households that kept the diffuser running after the trial ended, furniture scratching typically returned to its former level within two months.
The pheromone released by the diffuser closely resembles one that cats themselves deposit when they rub their faces against objects.
Operating a pheromone diffuser for a year costs more than buying several scratching posts.
Owners in the trial reported that their cats seemed calmer while the diffuser was in use.
Scratching is a natural behavior that helps cats keep their claws healthy.
questions.explanation: Scope shift: two weeks of results are used to support a 'lasting' solution. A shows the effect fades within two months even with the diffuser still running, which directly undercuts 'lasting.' B is the tempting trap; it explains how the diffuser might work, which supports the short-term effect rather than weakening anything.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The diffuser offers a lasting solution to destructive scratching.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a trial, scratching fell by about half in the two weeks after the diffuser was plugged in.

breakdown.analysis: Two weeks. Lasting? Those aren't the same thing. Cats might get used to the scent, and the effect could wear off. The argument stretches a short-term result into a long-term claim. It's like calling a diet permanent after one good week. We need an answer that shows the effect doesn't hold up over time.

choices.note: CORRECT. Even with the diffuser still running, scratching came back within two months. So the two-week drop was temporary, and 'lasting' is exactly what fails.
Tempting, because it's about the mechanism and sounds scientific. But it gives a reason the diffuser works. That supports the trial's result; it doesn't touch whether the effect lasts.
Wrong dimension. Cost doesn't speak to whether the solution lasts.
Calmer cats fit the claim that the diffuser works. If anything, a mild strengthener.
Interesting fact, but the argument is about whether the diffuser reduces destructive scratching for good, not whether scratching is natural or should be stopped.

questions.stimulus: Transportation official: Critics claim that raising the speed limit on the Calloway Expressway from 90 to 110 kilometers per hour has made the expressway more dangerous. Yet in the two years since the change, the number of collisions per million vehicle-kilometers traveled on the expressway has actually declined slightly. So the critics are mistaken: the higher limit has not made the expressway any more dangerous.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the transportation official's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses the rate at which collisions occur on the expressway with the total number of collisions that occur there
presumes, without providing justification, that raising the speed limit caused the decline in the collision rate
rejects the critics' claim solely on the grounds that the critics have not proven it
takes evidence about how often a kind of event occurs as conclusive about how much danger that kind of event poses
fails to consider that many drivers on the expressway may not obey the new speed limit
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the official's evidence concerns how often collisions happen, but 'more dangerous' also covers how severe they are, and crashes at 110 km/h tend to cause worse injuries. D names the move from frequency to overall danger. A is the most tempting trap, but the official deliberately uses a rate rather than a raw count, which is the appropriate measure; nothing is confused.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The higher limit has not made the expressway any more dangerous.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Critics say it has; but collisions per million vehicle-km have declined slightly in the two years since the change.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer collisions per kilometer. Fine. But is collision frequency the whole story of danger? A crash at 110 km/h is far worse than one at 90. You could have slightly fewer crashes and many more deaths. The official measures how OFTEN, then concludes about how DANGEROUS. That's a measure mismatch, a kind of scope shift. It's like saying a sport isn't dangerous because injuries are rare, when every injury is a broken neck. We need an answer that says frequency was treated as the whole of danger.

choices.note: Tempting, because traffic volume might have changed. But the official uses a rate (per million vehicle-km), which is the right way to handle volume. Using a rate isn't confusing it with a total.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions rose from 50 to 60, so the road's collision rate must have gone up, even though traffic doubled.

choices.note: The official only says danger didn't increase. That needs no claim that the higher limit CAUSED the decline.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Collisions fell after the limit rose, so raising the limit made the road safer.

choices.note: Tempting if you skim: it sounds like a rebuttal. But the official offers actual evidence (the collision rate), not just the critics' lack of proof.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Critics haven't proven the limit is dangerous, so it's safe.

choices.note: CORRECT. Collisions per kilometer measures how often crashes happen, not how bad they are. Higher speeds can make each crash deadlier, so 'not more dangerous' doesn't follow.
So? The conclusion is about what happened after the limit changed, whatever drivers actually did. Disobedience doesn't make the reasoning flawed.
